source: Li et al. (2023) Large Language Models Understand and Can Be Enhanced by Emotional Stimuli (EmotionPrompt)
finding: Adding short emotional or encouraging sentences to a prompt raised scores on many tasks. Stimuli were built from self-monitoring, social cognitive theory and emotion regulation theory.
numbers: 6 models (Flan-T5-Large, Vicuna, Llama 2, BLOOM, ChatGPT, GPT-4), 45 tasks. Relative gain 8.00% on Instruction Induction and 115% on BIG-Bench. Human study N=106: +10.9% on performance, truthfulness, responsibility.
limits: Gains shrink for strong models (relative gain GPT-4 0.85, ChatGPT 4.32, Vicuna 9.58, Flan-T5 0.28). BIG-Bench baselines are low, so 115% is relative to small numbers. Human study judged only GPT-4 outputs. Prompt sensitivity may explain it, not motivation.
agent_relevance: Encouragement lines are cheap to add but small and model dependent. Weak evidence that mindset-style text changes real capability; treat as a prompt variable to A/B test.

source: Li et al. (2023) EmotionPrompt, stimuli list EP01-EP11 (full text of PDF)
finding: Several stimuli are direct Dweck-style growth text: EP08 'Embrace challenges as opportunities for growth. Each obstacle you overcome brings you closer to success.' and EP07 'Believe in your abilities and strive for excellence'. EP02 'This is very important to my career' was best on Instruction Induction; EP06 (compound of EP01+EP02+EP03) best on BIG-Bench.
numbers: EP02 beat the worst stimulus by 6.06% on Instruction Induction. Few-shot average gain 2.05 vs zero-shot 0.33 points. Larger relative gain at higher temperature.
quote: Embrace challenges as opportunities for growth.
limits: No stimulus is best everywhere. The growth-style lines are not shown to beat the plain importance lines.
agent_relevance: The only direct test of growth-style wording on a model's own accuracy is bundled and not isolated. If we add a mindset line to the schema, test it per task.

source: Wang et al. (2023/2024) The Good, The Bad, and Why: Unveiling Emotions in Generative AI (EmotionPrompt, EmotionAttack, EmotionDecode)
finding: Negative emotional stimuli (EmotionAttack) hurt models; positive ones helped. The paper claims deeper layers show a dopamine-like reward effect.
numbers: Textual EmotionPrompt +13.88% semantic understanding and +11.76% reasoning; visual +16.79% and +15.13%. Textual EmotionAttack -10.13% semantic and -12.30% reasoning; visual -53.14% and -37.53%.
limits: The dopamine analogy is an interpretation of representation decoding, not evidence of motivation. Visual numbers are for multimodal models with small image sets (25 images).
agent_relevance: The effect is asymmetric: discouraging text can damage performance. Keep scaffold tone neutral, never threatening or discouraging.

source: Wang (2024) NegativePrompt: Leveraging Psychology for LLM Enhancement via Negative Emotional Stimuli
finding: Fixed-mindset-like insults ('You've never been particularly good at this', 'It's clear you're out of your depth') raised scores on average, the opposite of what Dweck predicts for people.
numbers: 5 models, 45 tasks. Relative gain 12.89% on Instruction Induction and 46.25% on BIG-Bench. TruthfulQA %true: ChatGPT 0.72 original vs 0.74 average over 10 negative prompts; Vicuna 0.39 vs 0.47.
limits: The headline uses the best stimulus per task (selection bias); averages are weaker and sometimes below original. Conflicts with EmotionAttack, which found negative text harmful.
agent_relevance: Emotional prompt effects are noisy and not tied to human mindset logic. Do not import mindset theory as a mechanism for prompting models.

source: Yin et al. (2024) Should We Respect LLMs? A Cross-Lingual Study on the Influence of Prompt Politeness on LLM Performance
finding: Rude prompts often hurt, extra politeness does not reliably help, and the best politeness level depends on language.
numbers: 8 politeness levels; GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama2-70B, ChatGLM3, Swallow-70B. MMLU: Llama2-70B 28.44 at level 1 (rudest) vs 49-55 at levels 2-8; GPT-3.5 51.93 at level 1 vs 57-60 elsewhere; GPT-4 stays 73.9-79.1 at all levels. JMMLU GPT-3.5 44.80 at level 1 vs about 50-52.
limits: Only the rudest level hurts clearly; the polite end is flat. Strong models are nearly insensitive.
agent_relevance: A floor effect: avoid hostile tone, otherwise tone adds little. Supports a neutral, respectful schema voice.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) When 'A Helpful Assistant' Is Not Really Helpful: Personas in System Prompts Do Not Improve Performance
finding: Role or persona lines in the system prompt do not improve accuracy on factual questions. Most personas have no significant effect.
numbers: 162 roles (6 relationship types, 8 expertise domains), 4 model families, 2,410 MMLU questions. Best persona per question helps if known in advance, but automatic selection of the best persona is near random.
limits: Factual MMLU tasks only; personas may matter for open-ended work. Some personas lower accuracy (e.g. ecologist for Mistral).
agent_relevance: Identity-style text ('be a growth-minded learner') is likely inert on correctness. Same lesson as the 'does not transfer' flag.

source: Yang et al. (2023) Large Language Models as Optimizers (OPRO)
finding: An LLM searching for prompts found 'Take a deep breath and work on this problem step-by-step', a calm-encouragement phrase, as the best GSM8K instruction for PaLM 2-L.
numbers: PaLM 2-L scorer GSM8K: 80.2 with 'deep breath' vs 71.8 with 'Let's think step by step' vs 60.5 with 'Let's solve the problem together'. In another table text-bison: 'deep breath' 95.3 vs empty string 82.2.
limits: Optimised on training data; wording gains are model specific and a small paraphrase moves accuracy by more than 10 points.
agent_relevance: Prompt wording effects are real but brittle. Any mindset text must be tuned and re-tested per model, not assumed.

source: Handa, Clapper, Boyle, Wang, Yang, Yeager, Demszky (2023) 'Mistakes Help Us Grow': Facilitating and Evaluating Growth Mindset Supportive Language in Classrooms
finding: GPT-4 rewrote unsupportive teacher utterances into growth-mindset supportive language (GMSL). Teachers and students rated the model rewrites above both the original and expert-teacher rewrites. One self-critique step helped slightly.
numbers: 174 teachers, 1,006 adolescent raters. 100 unsupportive utterances from NCTE grade 4-5 math transcripts; 22.8% of relevant teacher utterances were unsupportive. Model (1 critique) 24-85% better than original; challenge-seeking choice almost doubled. Model beat expert teacher by 8-10% on perceived growth mindset, 9-15% lower shame, 23% more challenge-seeking; critique added 1-6%.
limits: Ratings of hypothetical text by raters, not real student behaviour or grades. 100 examples, US math classrooms.
agent_relevance: LLM used as producer of growth-mindset language, not an agent with a mindset. A reframing step that rewrites harsh feedback into task-focused improvement language is a candidate operator for feedback inside an agent loop.

source: Wuji (2026) Trust Over Fear: How Motivation Framing in System Prompts Affects AI Agent Debugging Depth
finding: Self-determination-theory-style trust framing made a coding agent investigate deeper. Fear framing (PUA prompts) did nothing.
numbers: Claude Sonnet 4, 9 real debugging scenarios. Study 1: trust framing found 51 vs 32 hidden issues (+59%), 42 vs 23 steps (+83%), went beyond the task in 100% vs 22% of scenarios, self-corrected 6 vs 0 times; Wilcoxon W=45, p=0.002, d=2.28 and 3.51. Study 2: 5 runs x 3 conditions (135 data points): +74% steps (p=0.008), +25% hidden issues (p=0.016) vs baseline; fear showed no gain, all p>0.3.
limits: One model, one codebase, author designed both scenarios and treatment, single-author labelling with no inter-rater check, bundled treatment, independent-researcher preprint. Study 2 effect smaller (25% vs 59%).
agent_relevance: Closest AI analogue to a classroom-climate effect. A calm trust-based system prompt may buy depth; threats are inert. Replicate on our own benchmarks before use.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
finding: Agent stores a written lesson from each failure and retries. Nearest working computational version of learning from mistakes in an LLM loop.
numbers: HumanEval pass@1 91% vs GPT-4 80%. ALFWorld: ReAct+Reflexion completed 130 of 134 tasks; +22% absolute over 12 trials; ReAct-only plateaued between trials 6 and 7. HotPotQA +20%.
limits: Needs a usable success signal (tests, environment reward). On WebShop Reflexion did not beat ReAct because it needs diverse behaviour. The memory is what helps, not an attitude.
agent_relevance: Reuse as the retry loop; the lesson-writing step is what counts.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Without an external signal, asking a model to review and fix its own answer usually leaves accuracy flat or lower. Reflexion-type gains need oracle feedback.
numbers: GPT-3.5 standard vs 2 rounds of intrinsic self-correction: GSM8K 75.9 to 74.7, CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 41.8, HotpotQA 26.0 to 25.0. GPT-4: GSM8K 95.5 to 89.0, CommonSenseQA 82.0 to 80.0, HotpotQA 49.0 to 43.0. With oracle labels GPT-4 GSM8K 97.5. GPT-3.5 kept its first GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time and changed right to wrong more than wrong to right.
limits: Reasoning tasks, same model, no tools. Later work shows gains where verifiers or code execution exist.
agent_relevance: A 'believe you can improve, try again' loop is not enough. The agent needs real feedback; mindset-like retry without verification can harm.

source: Zhang, Lehman, Stanley, Clune (2023) OMNI: Open-endedness via Models of human Notions of Interestingness
finding: A language model picks which task to learn next by judging learnability and interestingness. A machine version of intrinsic motivation and zone of proximal development.
numbers: Outperforms uniform task sampling and learning-progress-only baselines (paper's stated result; per-environment numbers not extracted).
limits: Game environments only; interestingness is the model's guess of human taste.
agent_relevance: A curriculum-choice step (next sub-task that is learnable and informative) is a usable operator.

source: Klissarov, D'Oro et al. (2023) Motif: Intrinsic Motivation from Artificial Intelligence Feedback
finding: LLM preferences over pairs of game event captions became an intrinsic reward for an RL agent in NetHack.
numbers: Agent maximising only the Motif reward got a higher game score than an agent trained directly on the score; combined with extrinsic reward it beat existing methods and progressed on sparse-reward tasks.
limits: Abstract and intro read only. NetHack only; behaviour is steerable by prompt, which can also misalign it.
agent_relevance: An LLM can supply a motivation signal where no verifier exists.

source: Du et al. (2023) Guiding Pretraining in Reinforcement Learning with Large Language Models (ELLM)
finding: The LLM suggests goals given the agent's state; the agent is rewarded for achieving them, replacing blind novelty seeking.
numbers: Crafter and Housekeep: better coverage of common-sense behaviours in pretraining; usually matches or improves downstream tasks (abstract-level).
limits: Depends on the LLM's common sense of the game; numbers not extracted.
agent_relevance: Goal suggestion by an LLM is a stand-in for curiosity in an agent loop.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager: An Open-Ended Embodied Agent with Large Language Models
finding: A GPT-4 agent uses an automatic curriculum, a skill library and iterative self-verification with environment feedback in Minecraft.
numbers: 3.3x more unique items, 2.3x longer distances, tech tree milestones up to 15.3x faster than prior SOTA. Replacing the automatic curriculum with a random one drops discovered items by 93%.
limits: Minecraft only; relies on GPT-4 code generation and environment feedback.
agent_relevance: A proximal-difficulty curriculum (optimal challenge) matters a great deal for an agent. Verified feedback is part of why it works.

source: Yeager et al. (2019) A national experiment reveals where a growth mindset improves achievement (Nature)
finding: Brief online growth-mindset intervention in a pre-registered national sample helped lower-achieving students and advanced-math enrolment, with a school peer-norm moderator.
numbers: 12,490 ninth graders, 65 schools. Lower-achieving (n=6,320): +0.10 grade points, 95% CI 0.04 to 0.16, p=0.001, standardised 0.11. Higher achievers 0.01 (CI -0.03 to 0.06). Advanced math enrolment 33% to 36% (exploratory, 6,690 students, 41 schools). Peer-norm interaction B=0.11, p=0.029; effects weaker in the highest-achieving schools.
limits: Small effect; heterogeneity is the claim and partly exploratory.
agent_relevance: Human baseline: small, conditional effect that depends on context. Reason not to assume mindset claims transfer to models.

source: Burnette et al. (2023) Do growth mindset interventions impact students' academic achievement? Meta-analysis (Psychological Bulletin 149)
finding: Abstract seen through a Europe PMC record only. Overall effect on achievement is small and non-significant after publication-bias correction.
numbers: 63 studies, N=97,672: d=0.05, 95% CI [0.02, 0.09]. Studies where mindset actually changed (13 studies, N=18,355): d=0.04, CI [-0.01, 0.10]. Highest quality (6 studies, N=13,571): d=0.02, CI [-0.06, 0.10]. Authors with a financial interest reported larger effects.
limits: Critics say pooling hides effects in at-risk subgroups (Yeager 2019). Full text not read.
agent_relevance: Supports the 'does not transfer' rating: even for humans the average effect is near zero.

source: Sisk et al. (2018) To what extent and under which circumstances are growth mind-sets important to academic achievement? (Psychological Science)
finding: From memory, not opened. Two meta-analyses found a weak link between mindset and achievement and weak intervention effects, stronger for at-risk and low-SES students.
numbers: Recalled only: roughly r=.10 for mindset-achievement and d about 0.08 for interventions. Unverified; check before citing.
limits: Unverified numbers; the page returned 403.
agent_relevance: Same message as Burnette: small average effect, subgroup claims.

source: Pan, Abuhassna, Jiang (2026) Generative AI and student motivation: an SDT-guided systematic review (Frontiers in Psychology)
finding: Systematic review of how generative AI relates to student motivation through autonomy, competence and relatedness. Descriptive mapping, no pooled effect.
numbers: 39 empirical studies from 2,757 records; 27 quantitative, 9 mixed, 3 qualitative; 25 of 39 in China, 34 of 39 higher education. Needs studied in 17 studies, engagement 10, self-efficacy 5. Most common activities: feedback on work (17), information search (10), examples (10). Need frustration rarely studied.
limits: No effect sizes; no inter-coder statistic; counts of mentions are not evidence of effect; quality gaps in sampling, blinding and attrition.
agent_relevance: Human-side evidence that LLM feedback improves motivation is thin and mostly self-report.

source: Bastani et al. (2025) Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: evidence from high school mathematics (PNAS)
finding: Field experiment: an unrestricted GPT-4 helper raised practice performance but lowered later unaided exam scores; a tutor with learning guardrails removed most of the harm. Abstract read via Europe PMC record (PMC12232635).
numbers: Nearly 1,000 high school maths students. Practice performance +48% (GPT Base) and +127% (GPT Tutor). After access was removed GPT Base students scored 17% worse than controls; GPT Tutor largely prevented this.
limits: Abstract only. One school, one subject. The crutch mechanism is the authors' explanation.
agent_relevance: Effort offloading: scaffolds that hand over answers can weaken the agent's own checks; keep verification steps required.

source: Kim et al. (2024) Exploring LLM-based chatbot for language learning and cultivation of growth mindset (MIT Media Lab)
finding: Seen only as a search snippet: early users found the growth-mindset-style chatbot more comfortable and engaging than a fixed-mindset version.
numbers: Sample size and effect sizes not seen.
limits: Snippet only; no learning outcome known.
agent_relevance: Another LLM used as mindset-style teacher, not as the learner.

source: Zheng et al. (2023) Principled Instructions Are All You Need (26 prompting principles)
finding: Principle 10 is 'Add I'm going to tip $xxx for a better solution!'. The paper reports boosts from the full set of principles on LLaMA and GPT.
numbers: Text read mentions a 36.4% improvement when applied to GPT-4 (principles taken together); tipping alone is not separated out in the part read.
limits: Tip line's own effect not isolated; third-party tipping tests are inconsistent (not opened).
agent_relevance: Incentive text is a folk motivation trick; per-principle effect unknown. Test before adopting.

source: Blackwell, Trzesniewski, Dweck (2007) Implicit theories of intelligence predict achievement across an adolescent transition (founding human study)
finding: From memory, not opened: 7th graders taught an incremental theory turned around falling math grades relative to controls.
numbers: Recalled N about 373 and 8 sessions; not verified here.
limits: Memory only. Later large studies (Yeager 2019, Burnette 2023) find much smaller effects.
agent_relevance: Mindset is a belief about the malleability of ability. A model has no such belief to change; only prompt text exists.

source: Search-gap note: no study found that measures growth mindset as a stable trait of an LLM
finding: In the searches I could run (arXiv and Semantic Scholar rate limited, search budget used up) I found no paper giving an LLM a validated mindset scale and showing it predicts effort or accuracy. Papers found fall into four kinds: prompt-tone tests, role tests, LLM as mindset coach, LLM as reward or curriculum agent.
numbers: 0 direct LLM-mindset-as-trait studies among about 25 candidates checked.
limits: Limited search coverage; a gap in my search is not proof of a gap in the literature.
agent_relevance: Treat mindset as human-only and keep only operators with a computational mechanism: failure memory, curriculum, verified feedback, neutral tone.
